chapter: Family and growing up in Manhattan
title: Growing up on 64th Street: house rent parties and piano players
summary: He insists jazz and blues surrounded him as a child in the 64th Street neighbourhood, known as the jungles, with piano players heard along the street at night, well before Kansas City got the credit.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Of course there was no jazz when you first started. I mean there wasn't -- there was jazz but it wasn't around you I'm sure.
Well, oh, yes, it was. Oh, on the contrary, sure it was. I was aware of all different types of music, as I was coming up, you see. I came up in New York,
right down there on 64th Street, where I grew up, right here on 64th Street, between Amsterdam and West End. We used to call it the jungles.

And just those four or five blocks where the blacks lived in those days, you know, in that concentration, it was a hotbed of jazz and blues and everything else. I mean they publicized Harlem, but Harlem wasn't Harlem then. It was all down there where I was born, you know. And that's where the -- they used to call them the house rent parties and all that, and I remember very distinctly we'd go to bed at night and of course everything would be quiet and all you would hear was these piano players, all up and down the street, playing the blues and the boogie-woogie and all that stuff, you know. In later years, you know, they liked to credit this to Kansas City and this to this place and this to that place, but it had always gone on right here in New York.

Sure. Sure it was. Now, and this is in World War I I'm talking about. So naturally it was going on before that. Plus I remember in my house, you know, we always had a piano and instruments laying around, you know.
